title: 12,653 and Counting: Inside the Unstoppable Rise of Indian Restaurants Across America
excerpt: From classic New Jersey diners turning into biryani joints to vegan dosa houses in Phoenix, Indian cuisine is reshaping America's dining landscape at a pace not seen before.
body:
There are now 12,653 Indian restaurants operating across the United States, according to the latest data from POI Data, a business intelligence firm. California leads with 1,320 — roughly one in every ten — followed by Texas with 754. And the numbers are accelerating.

In December 2024 alone, 115 new Indian restaurants opened nationwide, according to market research firm Datassential. That's more than double the 54 that opened in September 2018. The growth tracks almost perfectly with the Indian-American population boom: the Pew Research Center reports that Indians in the United States have grown by roughly 3.1 million since 2000, an increase of 174 per cent.

But the story isn't just about more restaurants. It's about a fundamental shift in what Indian food in America looks and tastes like.

## Beyond Butter Chicken: The Hyper-Regional Wave

The Indian Restaurant Association of America flagged hyper-regional flavours as one of the top trends for Indian dining in 2025 and 2026. Chefs are digging deeper than the standard North Indian menu that has dominated American strip malls for decades, exploring the hundreds of local cuisines that dot the subcontinent.

In Fort Collins, Colorado, Bawarchi Indian Restaurant — known for authentic Hyderabadi flavours — is opening its second location to serve the growing communities in southeast Fort Collins and nearby Timnath. "Indian food was once at the bottom of the totem pole," said Sudheer Joshi, an Indian restaurant owner in Longmont. "But now people have gotten more educated."

In Phoenix, Desi Street Bytes has just opened with a menu of nearly two dozen types of dosas, idli, and Indo-Chinese fusion dishes — all 100 per cent vegan. It's a sign of how far Indian dining has moved from the all-you-can-eat lunch buffet stereotype.

## Diners Out, Biryani In

Perhaps no single story captures the shift better than what's happening on Route 1 in Edison, New Jersey — the heart of the Garden State's Indian-American community. The Menlo Park Diner, a classic 24-hour joint that opened in 1960, is being converted into House of Bombay, a new Indian restaurant expected to soft-open this month.

It's a symbolic moment. New Jersey diners — those greasy-spoon institutions with laminated menus and Frank Sinatra on the jukebox — are vanishing one by one, undone by rising labour costs, shrinking margins, and changing tastes. What's replacing them, increasingly, is Indian food. Edison's Oak Tree Road corridor is already one of the densest concentrations of Indian restaurants and grocery stores outside the subcontinent.

The conversion of the Menlo Park Diner into House of Bombay is less a loss than a generational handoff: the new American comfort food, at least in Central Jersey, comes with raita on the side.

## The Economics Driving the Boom

Several forces are converging. Indian grocery chains like Patel Brothers and Apna Bazaar have expanded aggressively, creating distribution networks that make sourcing spices and ingredients easier for new restaurateurs. Food delivery platforms have given small, regional Indian restaurants access to a customer base they could never reach with foot traffic alone.

Meanwhile, the fast-casual format — already proven by chains like CAVA for Mediterranean food — is being adopted by Indian concepts. The Indian Restaurant Association of America estimates that fast-casual Indian is the fastest-growing sub-segment of the market, attracting younger diners who want the flavour without the full sit-down experience.

Investment is following. According to Restaurant India, several Indian food and beverage brands are eyeing the American market for expansion, sensing that the infrastructure and consumer appetite are finally aligned.

## The Diaspora Angle

For Indian Americans, the restaurant boom is more than an economic story — it's a cultural marker. A generation ago, explaining "Indian food" to American colleagues often meant defending unfamiliar aromas and defending a cuisine that mainstream food media largely ignored. Today, Indian restaurants are earning James Beard nominations, Michelin stars, and NEXTY gold awards for grocery products.

The shift is generational, too. Second-generation Indian Americans are opening restaurants that speak to both their heritage and their American upbringing — places where dosas share the menu with craft cocktails, and where the design aesthetic is as considered as the spice blend.

## What's Next

The Indian restaurant count will almost certainly cross 15,000 within two years, if current trends hold. The real frontier is the mid-sized American city — Raleigh, Worcester, Columbus — where Indian populations are growing but dining options haven't caught up. For restaurateurs willing to bet on those markets, the math looks favourable: rising demand, lower rents, and a customer base hungry for something beyond the chains.
